Read About Saint Petersburg

A capital invented on a swamp, drawn with a ruler, and still keeping to the skyline its founders set.

A city that was decided before it was built

Most great cities grew. This one was decided. Peter the Great took a stretch of flooded delta at the mouth of the Neva — contested marshland with a Swedish fort on it and almost nobody living there — and announced a capital. The ground had to be raised before anything could stand on it, timber piles driven by the tens of thousands, canals cut to drain what could not be filled. The result is a city with no medieval tangle at its centre, because there was no medieval anything to build over.

That origin explains what a visitor actually notices first. Streets run straight and meet at planned angles. The great avenues were laid out as sightlines, aimed at a spire or a dome so the eye lands on something at the end of the view. Buildings sit in continuous terraces at a common height rather than competing for attention. It reads less like an old European city and more like a very large architectural drawing that was actually executed.

The flatness is the design. For most of the imperial period nothing was permitted to rise above the Winter Palace's cornice.

Why the skyline stays low

The rule was simple and it held for the better part of two centuries: no ordinary building could stand taller than the emperor's residence. Everything else — apartment blocks, ministries, banks, department stores — settled at roughly the same height beneath that ceiling. What breaks the line is deliberate: the gilded needle over the Admiralty, the cathedral spire inside the fortress, the dome of Saint Isaac's, the coloured onions of the Savior on Spilled Blood.

This is why a walkway forty-odd metres up gives you the entire centre rather than the roof of the next block. In a city of towers, a viewpoint at that height shows you a wall. Here it shows you the whole plan at once, and every landmark on it stands out precisely because the rule kept everything else down.

Water is the other half of the plan

The Neva splits into branches on its way to the Gulf of Finland, and the canals cut between them were working infrastructure long before they were scenery — drainage first, then transport. It leaves a centre where you cross water constantly without ever quite registering it as remarkable, and where the embankments, faced in granite, do most of the work of making the place feel monumental.

It also leaves a city that spends part of every year with its bridges up. Through the navigation season the main spans across the Neva open in the small hours to let shipping through, and the banks are genuinely separated until they close again. It is the one piece of local logistics that catches visitors out, and it is worth knowing which side of the river you are sleeping on.

The imperial collection, and what happened to it

The Hermitage began as a private gallery — a monarch buying European art by the crate — and grew into one of the handful of collections that define what a museum can be. It occupies the Winter Palace and the buildings strung along the embankment beside it, which is why walking through it means moving between two subjects at once: the paintings on the walls, and the state rooms, parquet floors and malachite columns holding them.

The city's other great interiors were built for the church rather than the court, and the most extraordinary of them replaces paint with glass. The Savior on Spilled Blood is lined almost entirely in mosaic, thousands of square metres of it, assembled tile by tile over more than two decades. Because the colour is in the material rather than on its surface, it has not faded the way frescoes of the same age have, and the room changes completely with the weather outside.

Siege is not a chapter here. It is the ground the modern city stands on.

The siege, and how the city carries it

For nearly nine hundred days in the Second World War the city — then Leningrad — was encircled and starved. Hundreds of thousands of civilians died, most of them in the first winter, and the survivors kept a functioning city running through it: a symphony premiered, museums crated and evacuated, the metro tunnels serving as shelters. The palaces in the suburbs were burned and looted, and the reconstruction that followed was measured in decades rather than years.

You will not find this presented as a tourist theme, which is part of the point. It appears instead in ordinary places — a plaque, a preserved warning stencilled on a wall about which side of the street was safer under shelling, a cemetery on the northern edge holding mass graves. It is the reason so much of what you visit is described as restored rather than original, and knowing that changes how the restorations read.

Reading the names

The city has been Saint Petersburg, then Petrograd, then Leningrad, then Saint Petersburg again, and each change was a political statement rather than an administrative one. The layers have not been tidied away: the surrounding region still carries the Leningrad name, and streets have variously reverted, kept their Soviet names, or acquired a third. A map from one decade will not entirely match a map from the next.

For a visitor this mostly matters at the point of navigation — a landmark may be signposted under one name, listed under another, and known locally by a third. It is less a source of confusion than a useful reminder that this is a place that has been renamed by every regime that held it, and has outlasted all of them.
